children: earnings per share are breaking out of a near-century-long historical trend, forcing investors to weigh whether the surge is a sustainable, AI-driven structural shift or a temporary capital expenditure bubble.

U.S. corporate earnings are currently experiencing an upside breakout that surpasses historic periods of economic growth, including the post-war boom, the globalization era and the tech revolution, according to a recent note from Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank Research.

EPS has remained within a stable long-term channel, growing at an annualized rate of around 6.5% between 1935 and 2019 despite multiple recessions, wars and inflation shocks. However, recent data show EPS surging well above this boundary, a trend analysts expect to continue in the coming quarters.
Reid noted that if sustained, this trajectory would represent one of the most significant structural breaks in modern market history, driven largely by the arrival of artificial intelligence

Despite the optimism, Reid offered a note of caution regarding how the data is measured. The analysis tracks EPS rather than aggregate corporate profits, meaning the numbers have been heavily boosted over the last two decades by corporate stock buybacks shrinking the overall share count. In fact, over the last 60 years as a whole, raw S&P 500
earnings have actually grown faster than EPS, he said.

"So going forward you have to take a side," Reid wrote. "Does AI allow for a sustainable breakout in earnings that no other technology or high growth period in the past has allowed, or is it a sign that we’re seeing an earnings bubble as the capex boom lifts all boats? The answer will impact every single global investor in the quarters ahead."
